name: Lighting Plots and Cue Design
title: Lighting Plots and Cue Design
answer: Lighting plots and cue design cover the documents and decisions that fix where light comes from, what it falls on, and when it changes during a performance or a shoot. A plot is the plan: instrument positions, types, colors, and channels, usually drawn over a ground plan of the stage or set. Cue design is the sequence: which lights change, in what order, at what speed, and on whose call. In virtual set work the same logic applies to digital lights and rendered environments, where the plot may describe software fixtures rather than physical ones.

A plot is the plan: instrument positions, types, colors, and channels, usually drawn over a ground plan of the stage or set. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The physical side runs on fixtures, dimmers, and a control console, with data carried over DMX or networked protocols such as sACN and Art-Net. Positions and focus are set during a paper tech and a focus session, then recorded as cues in the console's show file. Virtual production adds game engines and LED volumes, where lighting is authored in software and matched to the camera. Previsualization tools let a designer test a plot and a cue stack before anyone hangs a lamp.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with the script or shot list, a reading of where attention should sit, and a conversation with the director and set designer. The designer drafts the plot, assigns channels and colors, and writes cue synopses that describe intent in a few words. Cue numbers are built in rehearsal, refined at technical rehearsals, and locked before opening. Documentation matters as much as the look: a plot that a electrician can read at load-in is part of the craft.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights sit with the designers and programmers who authored the plot and the show file, and with the venue or producer under whose contract the work was made. Show files and plots are often treated as controlled documents, shared only with the crew that needs them. Safety rules govern rigging, electrical load, and work at height, and union agreements set who may touch the console. Where a design borrows a recognizable look from a film or another production, credit and permission are handled case by case.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Consoles and previsualization software keep absorbing more automation, from fixture libraries that populate a plot to cue suggestions drawn from a rehearsal recording. Virtual production pushes lighting design toward shared files between the stage and the render farm, so a cue can exist in both places at once. The open question is authorship: when a tool proposes a cue stack, the designer still signs the plot, and the paperwork has to say so.
